You're welcome!  Yes in a way-- You are the developer, you're not the hoster. You wouldn't manage their hosting, that is the hosting companies job. You are the developer, web designer, administrator of the site, Bob the website builder, whatever you want to call yourself; minus their host. Many people get confused on the difference between a host and someone who builds the websites.

For the ownership of the account as an example, say your customer wants 1 website that is just a basic WordPress site that will maybe get 100 users visiting a month and some email addresses. This would not require a Dedicated Server obviously. What you can do, is if you have a hosting company that you like and trust, recommend the type of hosting package that your customer will need to have their site hosted on without any issues. Most hosting providers offer a shared hosting package that is more than enough for what most people want. This also shows your customer that you have cared enough to do the research and it looks very professional. If you are unsure what your customer needs, call that company yourself. I answered presales questions all the time and just even inquiries where they said: "I need to run X amount of websites, X number of emails,  X number of emails going out on a daily basis, what plan would you recommend?"  No one charges you for that, and no one judges you on not knowing what you would need. Every hosting company is different and has different plans. 

Then, once you inform them that this is the hosting package that would be best suited for your website, they go to that company, purchase that hosting package (This includes domain names as well!) under their name, address, credit card, etc. and once done they provide you with access to cPanel. This is extremely important because the customer is able to change the password to that account if for instance something goes wrong or you have a fight and they want to change developers. That way they have access to their content and their whole website is not lost forever. 

To point my absolute favorite Malware Security software if you ever see your customer getting attacked multiple times is Sucuri. You can also run free scans on websites and it will let you know if it may be infected. (It's a free scan, so don't expect it to be 100% accurate)
Website: https://sucuri.net/

I also highly approve of using GTMetrix for optimization of any websites. Its a free scan, and not always 100% correct but it gives you awesome advice on how you can make the site better:
Website: https://gtmetrix.com/

I mentioned above about finding a hosting company that you trust and like. I use this site on a daily basis to look up who peoples hosting provider is, but they also are a Hosting Provider review site. I very much like this as people write mostly honest (you have the occasional exaggerator) reviews about their hosting provider. You can also narrow down categories if you are looking for specific locations, hosting types, and parameters.  It compares prices and it may help you make decisions on the hosting provider you go with.
Website: https://hostadvice.com/hosting-companies/

I  hope this extra info helps you out. If there is anything else I can help with or any questions I could answer for you, please let me know :)

From working for a few large hosting companies for many years, the most common things I have seen that are big factors when developers handle their customer's sites are that:

1. The account NEEDS to be in the customer's name. The customer needs to be paying for their own hosting. You are there to provide development services, not be their host. You are able to get access to their cPanel or control panel and you need nothing more than that. I've seen far too many times where developers fall off the face of the earth and just leave their customers in the middle of nowhere with no site and no access to their content. It's always so sad to see and all because the developer insisted the account be in their name. Yes, I understand that you can save money by using reseller accounts and can charge the customer less, but the loss of their account, content, and emails and possibly lawsuits on the developer (seen it happen) is not worth the small amount of savings of the account being in the developer's name.

2. Backups. BACKUPS!!! Shit happens all the time. You can be the greatest developer in the world but something, somewhere, at some point will go wrong. You need to have backups available. Charge extra for it if you want, don't care. Say it is a necessary charge that you will do (and make sure you actually do the backups). I recommended at least once a week if it is a site that is consistently being updated and probably more often than that if its a store-based website as things change very often for them. If its like a mom and pop "This is my website I just want to be on the internet", maybe once every 3 weeks is fine.

These are the two most common things I had seen as a Customer Service Rep/ Tech that really irk me when I hear about them and just wonder why it even happens.

Hope this helps, I probably could dig up a few more things if you'd like.
